The Great Lakes region is blessed with an abundance of water. But water quality, affordability, and aging water infrastructure are vulnerabilities that have been ignored for far too long. In this series, members of the Great Lakes News Collaborative, Michigan Public, Bridge Michigan, Great Lakes Now, The Narwhal, and Circle of Blue, explore what it might take to preserve and protect this precious resource. This independent journalism is supported by the Charles Stewart Mott Foundation. By Kate Furby | Michigan Public Toledo Zoo and Aquarium hosted the annual Sturgeon Fest last weekend. 1,200 visitors participated in the sturgeon restoration efforts. 1,500 baby sturgeon were released into the Maumee River to help historic sturgeon populations recover. Last Saturday was the annual Sturgeon Fest hosted by the Toledo Zoo and Aquarium. It was a striking scene, with people lining up to collect their six inch sturgeon in tiny buckets. Sign up Visitors waited in line for their turn to pour the baby fish into the Maumee River in Ohio. At the end of the line was a pair of small blue and white waterslides. Each visitor was helped by a teen zoo volunteer, making sure each small sturgeon was released to freedom in the river. Over 1,200 people attended. Live music, food trucks and educational booths celebrated the ancient Great Lakes fish. This sturgeon restoration program has been going since 2018, the year that Alyssa Cross was born. We spoke to her dad, Matt Cross, about the difficulty of juggling raising a family and baby fish at the same time in our podcast episode for Beyond the Shore earlier this year. You can listen to and watch the full episode here: Restoring the dinosaur fish of Lake Erie . The sturgeon have a complex life cycle that starts in rivers and moves into lakes as they age.
